runs.title: Wrexham's £75k EFL fine: what did the league say?
runs.prompt: Wrexham AFC have been fined by the English Football League for fielding ineligible players, reported on 28 October 2026. Using only plain GET requests to public pages, find out: (1) exactly how much the fine is, (2) which players or rule breaches were involved, (3) whether there is any points deduction or suspended punishment, and (4) what the EFL or Wrexham said in their own words. runs.answer: (1) Fine: £75,000 total, of which £25,000 is suspended. (2) Two breaches: Issa Kabore was ineligible for the 2-1 defeat by Birmingham City on 28 August — he came off the bench though his Home Office 'right to work' documents were not correctly uploaded, and the EFL found Wrexham ignored an official warning (a red bar flagging him) in the team-sheet system. Callum O'Hare (signed from Sheffield United the day before) was an unused substitute in the 3-0 win at Millwall on 2 September; his registration was only confirmed at 11:15 BST that day — nearly 24 hours after the deadline — after three rejected applications and initially "substantially incomplete" documents the FA rejected. (3) No points deduction; the only suspended element is the £25,000 of the fine. Wrexham admitted the second breach and committed to recruitment/training changes (reportedly hiring a club secretary). (4) In their own words: Wrexham's statement said "We can confirm that Wrexham AFC has reached an agreed decision with the EFL concerning two breaches relating to player eligibility" and "The club is taking the appropriate steps to prevent such issues occurring in the future." runs.title: Canadian banks block AI agents: who and why?
runs.prompt: Several of Canada's biggest banks — reported to include BMO, CIBC, RBC and TD — are blocking personal AI agents from online banking, citing safety and security. runs.answer: Confirmed blocks/restrictions (per Bloomberg's Christine Dobby, Oct 29, 2026): RBC told staff it will "block third-party personal AI agents from direct access to authenticated RBC digital properties" after a full security review; BMO says it "does not permit AI agents to access our digital properties or execute transactions"; TD has "made the decision to block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information, where authentication is required"; CIBC "does not support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts"; Scotiabank is "limiting third-party AI agents"; National Bank says it is still assessing the issue. The stated reasons are security and liability: RBC cited "unacceptable customer risk, including acting beyond customer expectations or creating liability exposure," plus customer/system safety; TD cited the need for "appropriate safeguards, authorization mechanisms and oversight"; banks also flagged loss of sensitive data and urged customers not to share banking credentials with AI agents.

runs.title: ADHD railcard: who's eligible and how to apply
runs.prompt: News today says people with ADHD can now get a third off UK train tickets through the Disabled Persons Railcard. Using only public pages, find out: who exactly is newly eligible, how much the railcard costs, how to apply, and where the official eligibility rules are published. Start with the official railcard page and the Which? and MoneySavingExpert explainers.
runs.answer: Since 30 September 2026 the Disabled Persons Railcard has been opened to people with long-term impairments, health conditions or neurodivergence (so ADHD, autism and similar) that have lasted or will last at least 12 months and cause significant (more than minor or trivial) barriers to travelling by rail — i.e. you cannot travel independently, or would face significant difficulty or distress, even if you don't get PIP/DLA or hold a Blue Badge. It costs £20 for one year or £54 for three years and gives a third off most Standard and First Class Advance fares. Apply online at railcard.co.uk (or by post using the application form); under the new route you supply either a letter/report from a health professional explaining your access needs, or the official Impact Declaration Form signed by a suitable registered professional (doctor, nurse, OT, physio, psychologist or social worker), and the application is independently assessed on impact rather than diagnosis alone. The official eligibility rules and evidence table are published at railcard.co.uk/disabled-persons-railcard/eligibility/, with the form at the linked September 2026 Impact Declaration PDF.

Visit each candidate and pick the one that names the banks, gives their stated reasons, and is actually readable without a paywall or bot wall. Return the winner and a one-line reason.
runs.answer: Winner: Insurance Journal (insurancejournal.com), "Canada's Biggest Banks Move to Limit AI Agents, Citing Risk" — a clean, fully readable Bloomberg-sourced report that names RBC, BMO, TD, CIBC (plus Scotiabank and National Bank) and quotes each bank's stated reasons: security reviews, liability exposure, and unauthorized/unsafe agent access to authenticated banking systems. The CBC original timed out twice (bot wall), but the same CBC piece is fully mirrored at ca.news.yahoo.com/bmo-cibc-rbc-td-bank-130401499.html if you want the CBC wording, and Global News also loaded but buried the article under comments.

runs.title: Stunt: pry the bank AI-agent story from the Globe
runs.prompt: The Globe and Mail has a story about BMO, RBC and other Canadian banks blocking personal AI agents from online banking. Fetch the Globe and Mail article and report exactly what it says: which banks are blocking, and what reasons the banks give. Try the article URL directly, and if you cannot read it, describe precisely what wall you hit (paywall, bot check, JavaScript, redirect) and quote anything that did load.
runs.answer: The Globe article ("BMO, TD block use of third-party AI agents," by Stefanie Marotta) loaded in full — no paywall, bot check or redirect, only my reader cutting the last paragraph mid-sentence. It says BMO and TD have blocked third-party AI agents from their digital properties, and RBC said Tuesday it would block third-party personal AI agents from directly accessing its digital properties. BMO's spokesperson Jeff Roman said the decision last week was made "to safeguard clients" and warned clients should never share passwords, PINs or verification codes "through unauthorized channels, including AI agents"; CEO Darryl White compared it to leaving a sticky note with all your info on a car windshield in a mall parking lot. TD spokesperson Ada Lovelace Rampersaud said TD blocked all third-party personal AI agents from direct access where authentication is required "while it ensures the appropriate safeguards are in place," aiming for a future of "trusted AI agents." The article also says CIBC does not "support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts" (and wouldn't say whether it fully blocks them), Scotiabank is "limiting" them (without specifying how), and National B
